canberra.title: Resident Evil is a near-perfect video game-to-movie adaptation
canberra.snippet: Any horror video game fan has, at some point, played a Resident Evil game. It is one of the most commercially successful franchises of al...
canberra.content:
Austin Abrams delivers a fantastic and hilarious performance as Brian in Resident Evil. Photo: Sony Pictures.

Any horror video game fan has, at some point, played a Resident Evil game.

It is one of the most commercially successful franchises of all time, with over 30 games in its catalogue dating back to 1997.

However, despite the acclaim and its status as a clear fan favourite, it has never managed to translate its popularity to film or TV.

Paul W. S. Anderson has made a series of movies starring Milla Jovovich, but they’ve never been anything more than low-budget cult classics.

Director Zach Cregger, of Weapons fame, has been tasked with bucking that trend with a fresh, high-budget reboot – and he knocks it out of the park.

Resident Evil centres around Brian (Austin Abrams), a medical courier. After delivering a vital organ to a hospital in Minnesota, he takes on one last job before wrapping up for the night: deliver a package to Raccoon City.

Fans of the early games will understand why that is such a challenge, but everyone else gets a firsthand look at why.

On his way into the city, Brian hits a woman with his car, but upon investigating the body, he quickly learns that something has happened to the evil residents (get it?) of the city.

Two things really work in this film.

First is Abrams’s performance. He is the perfect protagonist for a movie about survival. He has no clue what he’s doing or how he will survive the delivery, and that’s perfect.

Anyone who has played the games, especially the newer ones, understands the feeling of dread and uncertainty that comes with walking down every dark corridor or opening every blood-soaked door.

Abrams personifies this feeling while also being incredibly funny.

For a character that rarely interacts with anyone on his journey, he is genuinely hilarious. He consistently asks himself what the hell is going on and gets little to no answer. It’s honestly no different from how many gamers play the series.

It’s similar to his role in Weapons, which saw him as a homeless man trying to claim a missing-persons bounty, only dialled up.

The next factor is Cregger’s direction. It is clear he gets video games, and he gets Resident Evil.

The shifts between third- and first-person perspectives are ripped straight from the source material. The best example is when Brian uses a shotgun early in the film, and the camera essentially becomes a GoPro.

Cregger’s eye for horror is fantastic, too. He doesn’t rely solely on jump scares to deliver the chills. Instead, he uses lingering shots, slow camera pans and truly gross imagery to build tension. It’s fantastic.

There are a couple of gripes, and they do come in the final act. They aren’t movie-destroying, but they are mildly annoying.

Unfortunately, they relate to the biggest tie-ins to the games. Without spoiling, it centres on Brian’s interactions with survivors in the city.

They just aren’t from the same film. Brian has been through hell for the movie’s first hour and a bit; meanwhile, the people he meets are from a dark comedy.

The ending might also frustrate some, but for me, it perfectly wraps up where the movie was inevitably heading while also tipping their hat to the ending of one of the best games in the series.

Resident Evil continues 2026’s generational run of horror movies and adds another feather to Cregger’s growing filmography.

If Cregger stays committed to making these movies and the film hits its $80 million opening-weekend prediction (its budget is also $80 million), we’ll definitely be seeing more from the Resident Evil franchise.

Resident Evil is now showing in cinemas across the country.

canberra.title: Childcare safety breaches to go on public register as ACT steps up scrutiny of centres
canberra.snippet: Canberra parents will be able to check substantiated safety breaches and enforcement action taken against childcare centres under a new p...
canberra.content:
20 September 2026

Start the conversation

The ACT Government is considering changes to childcare legislation. Photo: Supplied.

Canberra parents will be able to check substantiated safety breaches and enforcement action taken against childcare centres under a new public register being developed by the ACT Government.

The register is among a series of reforms detailed in a government response tabled in the Legislative Assembly, alongside plans to significantly increase audits and quality assessments over the next two years.

The government is also considering whether to give the ACT childcare regulator another enforcement option by establishing an infringement notice system.

Children’s Education and Care Assurance (CECA) cannot currently issue infringement notices for offences under the National Law, meaning prosecution is the only option if it wants to pursue a financial penalty.

The government is examining the cost and viability of a fines framework, which would require legislative changes and new penalty, compliance and enforcement systems.

However, it says early scoping suggests a system for CECA alone may not be cost-effective, with existing powers such as suspension, cancellation and prohibition considered stronger deterrents for serious breaches.

The response follows a February motion from Independent MLA Thomas Emerson calling for reforms to improve safety and transparency in early childhood education and care. The motion included a public register of enforcement actions and greater regulatory scrutiny.

There are about 374 early childhood education and care services in the ACT, attended by more than 31,000 children.

CECA will establish a website with a register of specified enforcement actions that can be published under the National Law. Families will be able to see details of substantiated breaches and the action taken by the regulator.

“Families deserve to know the safety record of early learning centres they’re considering for their children,” Mr Emerson said.

“This is a huge win for transparency. We should have ready access to the information we need to make informed choices about the education and care of our children.”

CECA is also preparing to substantially increase its scrutiny of services.

The regulator estimates assessments and ratings will increase by 34 per cent by June 2027 and 50 per cent by June 2028 compared with 2025-26.

By June 2028, the ACT expects to meet the national benchmark of every service undergoing an assessment and rating at least once every three years.

Audits are also expected to increase from 210 a year by June 2027 to 280 by June 2028. The 210 audits would represent a 17 per cent increase on 2025-26.

The increased activity follows an $11.4 million investment over four years in the 2026-27 ACT Budget to strengthen regulation, including increasing CECA’s staffing capacity by more than 50 per cent.

The government has also committed to making child safety a renewed focus of the next phase of its early childhood strategy.

Education ministers are working nationally on educator-to-child ratios, including the “under the roof” approach, which can allow educators to be counted towards staffing ratios even when they are not directly working with a particular group of children.

CECA is also working with interstate regulators on concerns about providers with poor compliance histories taking over more centres through service approval transfers.

The government has also reaffirmed its push to increase the role of not-for-profit childcare providers in Canberra.

It has committed to having not-for-profit early childhood centres alongside all new ACT public primary schools and is using government facilities and below-market, peppercorn or concessional leases to support community providers.

Existing not-for-profit operators on peppercorn leases are being offered five-year tenure, while a new policy is being developed to prioritise community providers in government-owned early childhood infrastructure.

The government is also considering other measures to help not-for-profit centres compete with commercial operators, while acknowledging limits on using planning rules to restrict for-profit providers.

A final report on the reforms and an updated early childhood strategy are due in February 2027.

canberra.title: Are ‘smart’ cars making us stupid drivers?
canberra.snippet: On a recent holiday with a friend to French Polynesia, we hired a little Suzuki Jimny, circa 2018. For reference, I drive a 2024 Kia Sore...
canberra.content:
How can a car so small cause so much grief? Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

On a recent holiday with a friend to French Polynesia, we hired a little Suzuki Jimny, circa 2018.

For reference, I drive a 2024 Kia Sorento when at home. That was a significant departure from the bells and whistles I’ve grown accustomed to.

It also meant returning to a manual gearbox after 20-plus years of automatics. Also, I’d be operating the gearbox from the opposite side of the car. And the road.

No worries! I thought. It’ll come back to me.

Were there more sensible and more automated options available? Yes. But we opted for this iconic cutie for the vibes. We named her ‘Tahitia’. She had three doors, five speeds, a 1.5-litre engine and a seemingly unending ability to stress me out.

Because, as it turns out, driving a car is not like riding a bike.

Too much has changed. Modern cars have evolved into supercomputers on wheels with spaceship dashboards, thousands of sensors and paternalistic controls like lane assist and automatic braking.

Pulling out of the Avis parking lot, we were full of joi de vivre as we screamed around the island. Literally screaming with our mouths, you understand, because it was unexpectedly horrifying to drive on the right (read: wrong) side of the road.

Arriving at our accommodation, I was forced to attempt my first hill start as a born-again manual driver.

I did this while reversing into oncoming traffic as a distressed Francophone yelled at me. With each failed attempt, our little hire car inched closer and closer to flattening the surrounding fauna, and I watched my security deposit slip further from view. Eventually I found the car’s secret sweet spot between clutch and accelerator pressure and unlocked its ability to MOVE IN MY DESIRED DIRECTION!

Folks, it was at this moment I realised: There would be some worries.

From carefree cruising and feeling like a travel influencer to suddenly stalling with all the grace and vulnerability of an upturned turtle – in 0.5 seconds. Driving this Barbie jeep was a humbling experience. Photo: Hayley Nicholls.

Any skill I once possessed in mastering the art of revs had atrophied.

And is there anything more embarrassing than stalling a car? Nothing takes the wind out of your sails quite like it. With every stall, I went from Tropical Island Barbie to an upturned turtle until my ego shrank enough to fit appropriately in our pint-sized vehicle.

At one point, I turned the key enthusiastically (no ‘start’ buttons here) and another long-forgotten frustration resurfaced: the steering wheel lock. Never have I been so irrationally offended by an inanimate object.

Tahitia! Talk to me! What have I done? What do you WANT?

At this point, I effectively engaged in a physical fight with the car – twisting, pulling and pushing things at random.

Solving this puzzle ultimately cost us $50 in data roaming – and our pride.

But the most confronting discovery was just how much knowledge and skill I’d forgotten – or outsourced to my car – over the years.

As someone who generally bemoans the condescending, controlling nature of “smart” cars, I was surprised to find how reliant I’d become on their warnings and watchful eyes. I’ve become accustomed to being told when something is behind me, and resting in the knowledge that the car won’t actually let me hit it. Without reversing cameras or automatic braking, I felt incredibly vulnerable. Judging distance for myself suddenly felt like guesswork and totally irresponsible.

Forget swimming with reef sharks, carparks became the adrenaline rush of the trip.

So, are “smart” cars making us stupid drivers?

On a recent tour of a tertiary education institution, I learnt that students used to bring their own cars in to work on in their mechanics workshop, but are doing less and less as cars have become “too complicated” and “too specialist”. More computer than car.

Are the days of tinkering over? Is car maintenance soon to require an IT degree?

And for us drivers, has driving become a passive experience? Just another example of how technology – disguised as something helpful and beneficial – actually dumbs us down and turns activity into sedentarism.

Converting active pursuits into passive experiences, tech continues to simplify how we communicate, consume content and navigate the world.

For one nostalgic week, it was refreshing to feel like the driver, rather than a passenger in the driver’s seat.

That said, I stalled in traffic, got stranded on the roadside, and almost flattened an innocent Hibiscus.

Maybe Tahitia should have been driving.

canberra.title: Canberra’s newest thrift store to offer a second chance for more than clothes
canberra.snippet: A soon-to-open thrift store is set to make a difference in the lives of Canberra’s feline residents. The Canberra Street Cat Allian...
canberra.content:
Rescue volunteers are hard at work setting up the new thrift store ahead of next month’s opening. Photo: Canberra Street Cat Alliance/Facebook.

A soon-to-open thrift store is set to make a difference in the lives of Canberra’s feline residents.

The Canberra Street Cat Alliance (CSCA) was founded in 2014 to reduce street cat populations through adoption and its TNR (trapping, neutering and returning) programs.

For about a year, the alliance has been operating out of a new home in Crace, where it has leased a building once used by the CSIRO.

President Vanessa Parton said operating costs reached $200,000 in the last financial year, which was the highest on record.

To ease the burden, the alliance is opening a thrift store within its Crace home.

“As a self-funded rescue, we need to continue to improve our revenue streams,” she said.

“This just seems like it fits everything.”

The store will be called Rescued and Rehomed.

Ms Parton said calls to CSCA have been coming earlier than expected this year, as kitten season started early (when there’s an increase in the number of female cats giving birth).

“Already the requests for us – in terms of litters of kittens – are coming in. Pregnant street cats have been sighted,” she said.

“I’ve got five-week-old kittens and two-week-old kittens, as well.”

Ms Parton said profits would be used to support CSCA’s operations, including a plan to move to a home that it owns.

Once the store opens, it will operate as a traditional thrift shop, selling jewellery, DVDs, kitchenware, craft supplies, books and other items.

While they’ll also accept donations of pet items, the store won’t have an animal focus.

“Everything that you see in a thrift store, we will accept it, as long as it’s in good, clean, saleable condition,” Ms Parton said.

She said Rescued and Rehomed was inspired by a “phenomenal” garage sale CSCA held earlier this year.

“The support that we got from the Canberra public was huge,” she said.

“We had not just the cat lovers but members of the public that love a thrift store coming through.”

Since planning began, Ms Parton said CSCA members had been holding working bees to set up the store’s space.

The public can make donations at set times (advertised through Facebook) to make sure everything can be stored properly.

Ms Parton said people have already reached out to the organisation, wanting to donate.

“I think the fact that it is supporting Canberra Street Cat Alliance is appealing to a lot of the Canberra community,” she said.

“While they can’t adopt or they can’t help us trap … this is one small way that they can assist us.”

Rescued and Rehomed is set to open in October.

Canberra Street Cat Alliance’s permanent home is at 80 Bellenden Street in Crace. You can find out more (including donation drop-off times) by following its Facebook page.

canberra.title: Inside the cupboards helping Canberra ceramicists share some ‘little moments of joy’
canberra.snippet: Two blue cupboards are helping pieces of “leftover pottery” find homes. Several times a week, Amy Deep Blue Ceramics founder ...
canberra.content:
20 September 2026

Start the conversation

Amy Beggs-French hopes the ‘Clay It Forward’ movement brings joy to her fellow Canberrans. Photo: Lee-Anne Cooper.

Two blue cupboards are helping pieces of “leftover pottery” find homes.

Several times a week, Amy Deep Blue Ceramics founder Amy Beggs-French heads to the cupboards to drop off new pottery pieces.

“We just put a handful of pieces [inside the cupboards], and then every few days go and put another handful of pieces in,” she said.

“Some weeks we’re busier than others.”

She said the new initiative was a way to make sure ceramicists’ work doesn’t go to waste.

Inspiration struck when she realised studio members were making more items than they could take home – perhaps while they’re first starting out throwing pottery or while trying a new technique.

“There are some pieces that either get forgotten about, or they have a minor little flaw, or they’re just surplus to whatever needs and desires of the person who made them,” she said.

“Rather than see it go to waste, we decided that we would try and find new homes for these pieces of pottery that have been lovingly made, but then don’t have a loving home to go to for various reasons.”

Since the initiative started this winter, she estimated that “comfortably hundreds” of pieces have been adopted.

“It’s actually kind of crazy how positive the response has been.

“We’ve had people from the community just saying they absolutely love to walk the dog [past] or pop in and see what’s on offer.”

For Amy, most of the studio’s work is functional, meaning people can find mugs, bowls or cups in the cupboards.

“It isn’t a charity in a traditional kind of sense, and it’s not really about free pottery,” she said.

“The point is generosity without a transaction attached to it. It’s about a lovely idea that maybe there’s someone that you’ve never met spending some time making something.”

Beginner students make some, while professional makers donate others.

Amy said it means there’s a variety of styles and different kinds of items available for people to discover in the cupboards at any one time. But there are no holds.

“If a piece speaks to them, they’re welcome to take it for free,” she said.

“They find their way into our ‘Clay It Forward ‘ cupboards, and then they can be somebody’s favourite little dish … or they can use it to hold their jewellery in the bathroom.

“It’s pretty special to be able to share those little moments of joy that handmade clay can bring.”

The units themselves were given a second lease on life, after being obtained through a local ‘buy nothing’ group.

“The cupboards themselves have been upcycled … my husband is very handy, and he did them up for us. They’re drawers of a filing cabinet that have been repurposed.”

The two pottery cupboards are located in Weston, at the corner of Lycett Street and Souter Place, and at the corner of Gruner and Hildebrand Street. Learn more at Deep Blue Ceramics.

australia.title: The gunzels’ grand final: Melbourne Tramaroos’ campaign derails at European TramDriver Championship
australia.snippet: The Warsaw event saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired - to varying degrees - by tram drivers’ day-to-day tas...
australia.content:
It’s the grand final for gunzels. But despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne’s Tramaroos finished second last at this year’s European TramDriver Championship, just ahead of London.

The event, held in Warsaw on Saturday, saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired – to varying degrees – by tram drivers’ day-to-day work.

In smooth stop and go, drivers travelled with a bowl of water attached to the front of the tram – with points deducted for every drop spilled. Other precision tasks involved speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands.

Daniel Bowen, a spokesperson for the Public Transport Users Association, said it was “an unusual event in the pantheon of world sports”.

“It’s pretty entertaining,” he said, and an opportunity to look for inspiration from great other tram systems around the world. “Everyone looked like they were having a great time.”

This year’s title went to Vendula Tmejová and Zdeněk Rychtář, from Prague, in the Czech Republic.

In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to participate. This year, Yarra Trams sent Ivan Cavanagh of Southbank depot and Claudia Barrientos from Kew depot to compete as the “Tramaroos”. Had they won, the trophy would have gone “straight to the pool room”, Cavanagh said.

“You would hope our team would do well but I’m sure there’s pretty stiff competition against you know the Europeans,” Bowen said. “Perhaps it’s a bit like Eurovision – it’s great to participate.”

Thousands of fans followed the spectacle live in Warsaw, with about 80,000 viewers worldwide watching the competition via livestream.

Melbourne is set to host the next event in 2027.

Bowen said it would be interesting to see if other Australian cities joined the competition, given recent extensions to light rail systems in Adelaide, Sydney, Canberra and the Gold Coast.

“Back in Melbourne, it’s a reminder that trams do form a vital part of the transport system. We do have the biggest tram network in the world, but there’s more to do in terms of accessibility and on-road priority and service frequency.”

australia.title: One child dead and two children and woman in critical condition after Blue Mountains stabbing
australia.snippet: Crime scene established at Waratah Road, Valley Heights as NSW police say they ‘are not looking for any other people at this time’ Get ou...
australia.content:
A child has died in a stabbing attack in the Blue Mountains, with two other children and a woman in hospital in critical condition, New South Wales police say.

In a statement on Sunday afternoon, police said emergency services responded to reports of three children and a woman with stab wounds in a vehicle on Waratah Road, Valley Heights.

“Officers from Blue Mountains Police Area Command have been informed that several members of the public performed first aid on the woman and three children whilst contacting Triple Zero,” they said.

One of the children was found dead in the vehicle.

Police said NSW Ambulance treated the two children, who are believed to be under five, and the woman, believed to be in her 40s, at the scene before they were taken to Westmead hospital, where all three are listed as being in a critical condition.

“A crime scene has been established, and police are not looking for any other people at this time,” they said.

In a press conference on Sunday evening, Supt John Nelson said the two children and woman were undergoing surgery in hospital.

Nelson would not confirm whether the woman was the children’s mother but confirmed she was not known to police.

He said police had made contact with the children’s father, but not the wider family.

Nelson said the investigation was in its early stages, and appealed to the public to contact Crime Stoppers if they had dashcam footage or other information.

The officers who responded to the incident had support available to them, he said.

“Like any human being it’s a tragic circumstance to be exposed to,” he said.

australia.title: Three men charged with domestic violence-related murders after three women killed in separate incidents in NSW
australia.snippet: A Bondi Beach woman in her 90s, a 23-year-old in Wagga Wagga and a woman in her 70s in Mole River died within hours of each other on Satu...
australia.content:
Three men have been accused of domestic violence-related murders after the deaths of three women in New South Wales on Saturday.

Sergei Mitnik did not apply for release on Sunday when he appeared in a bail court hours after being charged with the murder of an elderly woman inside a unit at Sydney’s Bondi Beach.

The woman in her 90s was found with significant stab wounds to her torso about 5.15pm on Saturday. She died at the scene.

Mitnik, who police said knew the woman, was arrested at the home before being charged with domestic violence-related murder.

Defence lawyer Javid Faiz said the event was “extremely serious”, adding there were concerns about his client’s mental health.

He noted an appointment with a psychologist was cancelled a month ago and his client had been taking the medication Ozempic, which “had an effect on him”.

There was no application for bail and the case was adjourned to Thursday.

Hours before the elderly woman’s death, a 23-year-old died after being found with stab wounds inside a home in Wagga Wagga, in southwest NSW.

Adam Mark Perrim, 31, was arrested almost nine hours later at another home in the regional city and was later charged with the young woman’s murder.

The pair were in a relationship, investigators said.

He briefly appeared before court on Sunday but did not apply for bail.

The 31-year-old will next appear in court on 18 November.

Later on Saturday, the body of a 70-year-old woman was found at Mole River in the state’s north after reports of a domestic violence incident in the regional district about 9.35pm.

Police believe a 37-year-old man entered a property and tried to steal a vehicle before assaulting a 74-year-old male resident.

The younger man was arrested and police then went on to search the neighbouring property, where they discovered the woman’s body.

Part of the house was damaged by fire, police said.

The 37-year-old man has been charged with murder and is due to appear before court on Monday.

Police said he and the woman also knew each other.

Premier Chris Minns said his thoughts were with the families and communities of the three women.

“These are shocking crimes and families are today dealing with unimaginable grief,” he said.

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said as “these matters are before the courts, I won’t comment on the circumstances. But we cannot treat this as background noise”.

Sloane said Australia was “failing women across our country and every level of government, and every one of us, has a responsibility to act”.

“These deaths are not isolated. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25 by her intimate partner. Even more women lose their lives when you include other family members,” she said.

“Women of every age, from a 23-year-old to a woman in her 90s, are still not safe in their own homes.”

australia.title: Melbourne finishes second-last at world tram driving championships – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The prime minister has been asked if Australia has a...
australia.content:
Melbourne finishes second-last at world tram driving championships

Despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne tram drivers finished second last, just ahead of London, at the 12th European TramDriver Championship held in Warsaw yesterday.

A team from Prague finished first out of 26 teams, at the highly demanding course, which included: smooth stop and go, speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands.

Melbourne will host the next event in 2027. In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to compete in the competition.

What we learned, Sunday 20 September

We’re closing our live coverage there today. Here’s what we covered:

  • A child has died in a stabbing attack in NSW’s Blue Mountains, with two other children and a woman in hospital in critical condition.

  • The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says women are being failed “across our country and [by] every level of government” after the deaths of three women just hours apart in separate incidents.

  • Anthony Albanese says he hopes for engagement between the US and Chinese presidents on AI at the UN general assembly next week. He also said Apple’s executive chair, Tim Cook, had praised Australia’s under-16 social media ban.

  • The prime minister said One Nation’s immigration policy would be “diabolical” for the economy.

  • Angus Taylor said the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, should “get on board” with opposition promises to introduce a “fuel price shield” and lower the tobacco excise.

  • Melbourne tram drivers finished second last, just ahead of London, at the European TramDriver Championship held in Poland.

Thank you for joining us, we’ll be back again tomorrow.

One child dead in Blue Mountains stabbing, two children and woman in critical condition

A child has died in a stabbing attack in the Blue Mountains today, with two other children and a woman in hospital in critical condition, New South Wales police say.

In a statement this afternoon, police said emergency services responded to reports of three children and a woman with stab wounds in a vehicle on Waratah Road, Valley Heights. They said:

Officers from Blue Mountains Police Area Command have been informed that several members of the public performed first aid on the woman and three children whilst contacting Triple Zero.

One of the children was located deceased in the vehicle.

Police said NSW Ambulance treated the two children, who are believed to be under five, and the woman, believed to be in her 40s, at the scene before they were taken to hospital, where all three are listed as being in a critical condition.

“A crime scene has been established, and police are not looking for any other people at this time,” they said. Police are urging anyone with information or mobile phone or dashcam footage of the incident to contact Crime Stoppers.

Plibersek says ‘we owe these women more than our sorrow’ after deaths in NSW

The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has made a statement after the deaths of three women in alleged domestic violence-related murders in separate incidents in a 12-hour period in NSW.

Three men have now been charged with domestic violence-related murders. They include a 37-year-old man charged today after the body of a woman in her 70s was found at Mole River in the state’s north yesterday evening.

In a statement, Plibersek said her thoughts were with the families and loved ones of the women:

We owe these women more than our sorrow.

Every level of government, every community organisation, our schools and workplaces, every family – all of us need to work together to keep women and children safe.

Treasurer warns of ‘confronting’ 40-year economic outlook

Sarah Basford Canales

Australia’s 40-year outlook will be “confronting”, treasurer Jim Chalmers says, but not a “pessimistic story” as AI looks to transform the global economy.

Chalmers will present the seventh intergenerational report tomorrow afternoon, detailing forecasts for the impact of new technologies on society and the economy, along with more warnings about the country’s ageing population and declining fertility rates.

It comes as the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is visiting the United States this week to discuss a “global framework” for the rollout of AI, urging the “big two giants” – the US and China – to work in the interest of humanity.

At a press conference this morning, the treasurer warned the report will show Australia is “dealing with serious risks to our economy and serious pressures on the budget” but he believed the government’s policies were well-equipped to handle it.

The intergenerational report is a really important way that we plan for the future to make sure that Australians are beneficiaries and not victims of all this accelerating change that’s come at us from around the world.

AI will be the most “transformative influence on our society and our economy over the next 40 years”, Chalmers said.

Artificial intelligence does present us with very substantial risks that we will manage. I’m very confident that we can maximise the economic upside of technological change at the same time as we minimise the very substantial risks and concerns that people legitimately have about how this part of our economy is changing.

Melbourne finishes second-last at world tram driving championships

Despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne tram drivers finished second last, just ahead of London, at the 12th European TramDriver Championship held in Warsaw yesterday.

A team from Prague finished first out of 26 teams, at the highly demanding course, which included: smooth stop and go, speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands.

Melbourne will host the next event in 2027. In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to compete in the competition.

Damaging winds expected throughout Tasmania and parts of Victoria today

The Bureau of Meteorology has issued severe weather warnings in both states with north-westerly winds expected to increase on Sunday ahead of a strong cold front.

Peak wind gusts around 90-100km/h were forecast, and already recorded in some locations. A 109km/h wind gust was recorded at kunanyi/Mount Wellington in Hobart earlier this morning. While in Victoria, a 95km/h wind gust was recorded at Mount Gellibrand, about 130km south-west of Melbourne.

Maximum temperatures on Sunday were expected to reach 8C to 15C above average across south-east Australia, the BoM said.

By midday, temperatures had already exceeded 35C at several locations across the country, including Oodnadatta in South Australia, Birdsville in Queensland and at Roebourne airport west of Port Hedland, in WA.

Ten historic Sydney train stations ready for metro extension opening

The stations are now ready to reopen as metro stations ahead of the extension of the wildly popular line later this year, the NSW government says.

The ten stations – Marrickville, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Canterbury, Campsie, Belmore, Lakemba, Wiley Park, Punchbowl, and Bankstown – used to form part of the 130‑year‑old heavy rail line. They have been closed since September 2024 in favour of rail replacement buses.

The government says the now complete metro refurbishment has required the installation of 360 automated platform screen doors, and more than 1,300 gap fillers to fill the spaces between the trains and curved platforms.

The NSW transport minister, John Graham, says:

These 19th-century stations have transformed to meet the standards of the 21st century public transport.

These station upgrades are the culmination of years of hard work, investment and patience from their communities. Along with every person living in this corridor, I can’t wait to see these stations in full swing.

The government has declined to provide a state date for the Sydenham to Bankstown extension before the national rail safety regulator approves the line. The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that Sydney Metro is targeting a public opening date in mid-October.

Sloane says says women being failed after three deaths hours apart

The NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, says women are being failed “across our country and [by] every level of government” after the deaths of three women just hours apart in separate incidents in NSW.

They include the death of a woman in her 90s, who was found with stab wounds inside her unit at Sydney’s Bondi beach at about 5.15pm yesterday. A 47-year-old man has been charged with murder.

In a statement this morning Sloane said she was horrified by the deaths.

These deaths are not isolated. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25 by her intimate partner. Even more women lose their lives when you include other family members …

Because these matters are before the courts, I won’t comment on the circumstances. But we cannot treat this as background noise. We are failing women across our country and every level of government, and every one of us, has a responsibility to act.

In a statement today, the premier, Chris Minns, said “these are shocking crimes and families are today dealing with unimaginable grief”.

My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of the women who have died, and the communities affected by these events.

Petra Stock

South Australian algal bloom caused sea dragon mass mortality event

Thousands of sea dragons, pipefishes and seahorses died during South Australia’s devastating algal bloom, in what ecologists say is the worst mass mortality event for the fish family globally.

More than 1,600 weedy and leafy sea dragons, 1,400 pipefishes and 160 seahorses washed up as the harmful algae spread along the state’s coastline, according to analysis of citizen scientist records by Dragon Search SA.

The state is home to more than 30 species of Syngnathidae, a family that includes sea dragons, seahorses, pipefishes and more. At least 13 were affected by the toxic bloom, which began in March 2025 and still lingers at one site in southern Spencer gulf.

Weedy and leafy sea dragons, found only in Australia, were often some of the first mortalities observed, as the algal bloom spread up and down the coast.

Read more here:

Sarah Basford Canales

Opposition leader says treasurer should ‘get on board’ with his tax cut plans

Angus Taylor has continued to spruik his double tax cut policy this morning, which he claims will lower petrol prices and put the budget in better shape.

On 2GB radio, the opposition leader said the treasurer, Jim Chalmers, should adopt the policy to halve the fuel excise when the two-week average price of oil exceeds US$100 a barrel and cut the tobacco excise to take back cigarette sales from the black market.

Chalmers told News24 this morning the government had no plans to again halve the fuel excise as oil prices continue to rise in response to the US’s protracted conflict with Iran.

Taylor said:

Let’s just lock it in, and let’s stop this silly carry on. And the treasurer should just get on board. He should just get on board, and this is a treasurer who’s in denial about the state of the economy.

Taylor insists fuel price shield policy is ‘anti-inflationary’ after Chalmers labels it ‘uncapped, unfunded’

The federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, has insisted his “fuel price shield” policy is “anti-inflationary” after criticism by the federal treasurer, Jim Chalmers.

As we reported earlier, the opposition’s policy would see the federal fuel excise halved when the two-week average price of oil exceeds US$100 a barrel.

Asked what he thought of the idea on News24 earlier, Chalmers accused Taylor of coming up with an “an uncapped, unfunded policy”.

Angus Taylor’s not trying to save Australian motorists from higher petrol prices. He’s trying to save the Liberal party from One Nation.

At a press conference this morning, Taylor rejected Chalmers’ comments, saying the opposition would fund the policy through increased revenue created by controversial proposed cuts to the federal tobacco excise.

We can bring down taxes, fully fund it through the budget, and ensure that we provide the relief Australians want at the bowser: $15 a tank, 27 cents a litre … So this is anti-inflationary, and it’s been done in a way which is responsible for the budget.

The opposition has estimated the policy would cost around $950m each month, and would have been triggered twice in the past five years, during oil price shocks in early 2022 and March this year.

Albanese says One Nation migration policy would be ‘diabolical’ for economy

The prime minister has defended the government’s proposed immigration enforcement rules, as One Nation and the Coalition call for a tougher crackdown on net migration.

The government has announced long-awaited changes to immigration rules, under which foreign nationals without a valid visa face new measures to force them to leave the country. It has promised to bring down net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year, and 225,000 in 2027-28.

One Nation says it is targeting net-negative arrivals over three years, while the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, told the NSW Liberal state council yesterday he would introduce one of the “biggest immigration cuts in Australian history”.

Albanese told the ABC’s Insiders One Nation’s policy would be “be diabolical for our economy, and have real consequences for issues such as aged care, healthcare, the hospitality sector, the agricultural sector”.

A poll by The Sydney Morning Herald suggested 40% of voters thought the government’s 2027-28 target was still too high. Asked about recent polling on immigration, Albanese said:

We will put forward the case, for example, of our farmers need the areas to come in if they’re going to have their crops picked. That is just something that the farming sector are telling us, and it’s something that’s a reality, as well as [in] a range of other areas as well, including in the care sector.

australia.title: Rapists could face life in prison and barristers be prevented from ‘putting victims on trial’ under Victorian Labor reforms
australia.snippet: Premier Ben Carroll says if re-elected Labor will legislate a new form of manslaughter and increase maximum penalty for rape to life impr...
australia.content:
Rapists could face life sentences and lawyers would be prevented from asking humiliating questions of victim-survivors under a suite of Victorian Labor pre-election commitments designed to reduce violence against women.

The premier, Ben Carroll, on Sunday announced an election commitment to legislate a new form of manslaughter covering cases in which a person takes their own life as a result of family violence, as well as a new offence covering perpetrators abandoning a victim in need of medical care.

The state government also plans to change the law to let courts consider patterns of sexual abuse as evidence at trial and stop barristers using “humiliating and invasive questioning techniques” in court.

“I’m sick of Victoria’s courts and defence barristers putting victims on trial,” Carroll told reporters on Sunday.

The maximum penalty for persistent family violence intervention order breaches would also be doubled to 10 years’ jail under Labor’s pitch.

The government said the two new offences would close “loopholes” that allow perpetrators to “slip through the cracks in the justice system and walk free”.

The government has also committed to increasing the maximum penalty for rape from 25 years to life imprisonment and upping the maximum penalty for every other serious sexual offence by five years. The maximum penalty for persistent breaches of family violence intervention orders would also double from five years’ imprisonment to 10.

It will also make the standard sentence for the murder of a current or former partner 30 years – up from 25.

The proposed offence criminalising the abandonment of victims in need of medical care responds to recommendations made by the coroner after the deaths of Belinda Jones and Narelle Simmons.

Jones, 40, died on the floor of her Maryborough home in July 2023 after her partner left her there overnight and then waited two hours to call an ambulance after waking to find her cold and not breathing.

Jones had succumbed to treatable bacterial infections and sepsis, which a hospital failed to diagnose during an emergency presentation days earlier. Her partner was not charged with any offence in relation to her death.

In her findings published last month, the state coroner, Liberty Sanger, said: “In my view, the act of abandoning a victim of family violence requiring medical attention is an act of family violence, that instils fear in the victim and affirms a perpetrator’s control over the victim.”

Simmons, 42, died in October 2021 after her partner admitted to punching her twice in the face and elbowing her once in the back of the head before leaving her Cranbourne home.

Her body was found nine days later after her daughter requested a welfare check. Sanger was unable to determine whether she died immediately after the assault or hours or days later.

Her partner – whom the coroner said had 18 previous family violence victims – pleaded guilty to common assault and failing to report a reportable death. He was sentenced to five months’ imprisonment and a 12-month community corrections order.

The government’s announcement comes after a week of crime-focused election commitments from Carroll, including creating a new police training facility in Melbourne’s western suburbs and the introduction of Jack’s Law, which would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors.

“I’m a tough-on-crime premier – and that means being tough on family and sexual violence,” Carroll said in a statement before Sunday’s announcement.

“We must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks.”

The Coalition last year committed to Jack’s Law and also have plans to expand adult sentencing for youth offenders, increase police numbers and split the existing court of appeal into two separate entities, if elected in November.

world.title: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say
world.snippet: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump admini...
world.content:
Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.

The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.

Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.

The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.

The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.

Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.

Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.

The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.

The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.

In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone ​so he could contact relatives and a ​lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.

In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.

In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.

“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.

In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”

Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.

Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.

Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.

Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.

A spokesperson for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said that “when an individual is no longer in ICE custody, ICE is no longer responsible for them”, adding: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country.” The agency did not engage with questions about the violence deportees have faced.

A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”

The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.

“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

world.title: Survivors recount panic and struggle to breathe in Nigerian prison cell where 37 died
world.snippet: Police fire teargas as protests break out in city of Minna after deaths of suspected illegal goldminers, many of whom were children Survi...
world.content:
Survivors from a prison cell in Nigeria where 37 suspected illegal goldminers died while in the custody of a paramilitary group this week have recounted their panic and struggle for breath, as police on Friday fired teargas at people protesting against the deaths and imposed an overnight curfew in the city of Minna.

The victims – many of whom were children – were found dead on Thursday in the cells of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), which had raided suspected illegal goldmines and ⁠locked up dozens of miners in the city, the state capital of the mineral-rich state of Niger.

NSCDC – a paramilitary group that works with police – initially blamed the deaths on a disease outbreak. However, an intelligence report seen by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said preliminary information suggested that overcrowding and inadequate ventilation were responsible.

The state governor, Umar Bago, said many of the dead were children, aged 14 to 18, who had been working in the mines instead of going to school. “There are issues of illegal mining and it is taking a toll on our children,” he said.

Dauda Shehu, a survivor from the cell, told journalists at a hospital on Friday: “We were jam-packed in the cell, no ventilation for us to breathe well. All of a sudden we realised that we could not breathe and we were all scampering for where to get fresh air, we even appealed to them several times, banged the cell door, but they refused to answer us.”

A video shared online showed the bodies of dozens of young men clad only in shorts, most of whom appeared to be teenagers, sprawled on the ground out in the open. Volunteers wearing gloves can be seen standing over the dead, while veiled women try to identify the bodies of their relatives. Voices shouting curses on those responsible can be heard in the background.

AFP reported that another survivor, who asked not to be named, said he had made it out alive because he was near the cell’s entrance, where he could breathe better. “We were screaming for help,” he said, with detainees telling the guards that “people are dying one after the other. They did not believe us.”

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu ordered an investigation into the deaths after his government earlier suspended some senior officials.

But protests over the deaths broke out on Thursday evening in Minna. On Friday dozens of young people, including miners and their relatives, gathered near the NSCDC’s office in the city. Police cordoned off the area and attempted to disperse the protesters by firing teargas.

A Reuters witness saw security forces fire live rounds as protesters – ​some armed with sticks, machetes and traditional hunting rifles – called ‌for justice. Some protesters tried ‌to set fire to government buildings in the Tunga neighbourhood. “We are not thieves – we are simply seeking a way to make ‌a living by mining,” Yusuf Auwal, a miner who joined the protesters, told Reuters. At least one body lay on the streets. Soldiers and police officers patrolled Minna to try to restore order.

As ⁠curfew began at 6pm local time on Friday, security forces appeared to have at least temporarily restored order to the streets of the city.

The NSCDC said the detainees had been held in raids on suspected illegal mines on 15 and 16 September in the Wushishi-Lukoto area west of Minna. Nigeria’s interior minister, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, ordered the immediate suspension of Niger state’s NSCDC commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, pending the outcome of an investigation.

Niger state, which is Nigeria’s largest and is more than twice the size of Belgium, is rich in minerals and attracts thousands of artisanal miners, most lured by gold.

Police and the NSCDC did not initially provide a precise number of deaths but the state governor, Mohammed Umaru Bago, later confirmed 37 people had died.

“It’s so sad, it’s so tragic,” he said, adding an inquiry into the deaths had already started work. He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections due in January. The men were buried on Thursday, according to Islamic tradition, without any forensic investigations.

The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state is fuelling violence by criminal gangs, according to officials and experts. The gangs tax the miners and demand a cut from the extracted ore as a levy to allow them access to the pits.

Most of the illegally mined gold is smuggled to the United Arab Emirates, where it is laundered into the global supply chain in Europe, the US, Asia and South Africa, according to a 2024 Swissaid report.

Apart from gold, the state of Niger sits on deposits of other minerals including tantalite, copper and lithium, which are in strong demand for use in electric vehicles and clean energy technology.

Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

world.title: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout
world.snippet: Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week A British woman kid...
world.content:
A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.

Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.

Malawian police announced Osman’s rescue late on Thursday in a statement. “There was an exchange of fire between police and kidnappers, who were armed with [an] AK47 rifle and a Girsan Regard MC pistol. In the process, the criminals got shot and were taken to hospital where they succumbed to their injuries.” it read.

A police officer, deputy inspector general Mlowoka Noel Kayira, was also shot during the operation. “He is currently receiving medical attention at the hospital and is in a stable condition,” police said.

Osman, a 47-year-old auditor and mother of two, was safe and “not too shaken” after her ordeal, her brother Shobi Jiwa told the Sun, expressing his gratitude to Malawi’s police.

Jiwa reserved special thanks for Kayira. “He is the hero of our family. He’s the hero of the country,” he said. “He’s the hero of the world, actually, for putting his life at risk and taking a bullet into himself for my sister.”

Kidnappings are rare in Malawi, which has experienced a rise in pickpocketing and house burglaries by often armed men in recent years amid unstable, crisis-ridden economic conditions.

The landlocked southern African country is one of the world’s poorest nations, with a population of about 22 million and an average annual income of just $672, according to the World Bank.

In 2024, a country report by the US state department’s diplomatic security service said: “Kidnappings are not a widespread concern in Malawi, and there have been no recent high-profile incidents involving westerners.

“Historically, expatriates have not been significant targets for kidnappings in the country. When kidnappings do occur, they often involve members of the Asian business community rather than foreign travellers or residents.”

Osman, who is originally from Leicester, worked for a local audit firm and had lived in Malawi with her husband and children for several years. Before her rescue, her family said they had not had any news of her, including any contact from the kidnappers demanding a ransom.

Her husband, Nazil Osman, told the local news outlet Nyasa Times: “I don’t know where she is or how she is. My wife is an auditor, and I have no issues with anyone.”

Her brother told the Sun on Tuesday: “My sister has been missing for five days with no trace or call,” adding that the family could not think of a motive for her kidnapping.

Police did not say whether information received in response to the offered reward had led to Osman’s rescue, adding that investigations were ongoing and more details would be shared “in due course”.

world.title: Louisiana firefighters find feline native to sub-Saharan Africa while responding to house fire
world.snippet: The African serval, illegally enclosed in the back yard, was subdued and transferred to an animal welfare facility Louisiana firefighters...
world.content:
Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, prompting an animal welfare agency to seek placing the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.

Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.

A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws in effect in Marrero require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.

The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.

Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.

Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.

Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.

They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.

A social media post on Friday by Brignac said JPaws had managed to place the serval with a zoo “where he could have something very different: space, enrichment, appropriate care and an environment designed with his needs in mind”. Brignac’s post did not specify to which zoo she was referring.

The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.

Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.

That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.

In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.

And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.

The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

world.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
world.snippet: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech...
world.content:
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.

It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.

The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”

Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.

“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

Earlier this year, PEN International launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”
